CIAO THERE. It’s Gerardo Fortuna, fresh from Portugal Day celebrations where European Council President António Costa shared the bill with the Schumaniacs, a rock band made up of legal advisers from embassies and institutions whose motto is “legally sound.”

In today’s Playbook:

— The last MEP facing prosecution in the Huawei scandal fights back.

— Can a 36-minute psychometric test determine who climbs the Commission ladder?

— Faces in the crowd: Philippe Léglise-Costa, Fulvio Martusciello, Maria Walsh, Valerio Ottati, Cristiano Sebastiani, Pedro Lourtie, Maria Luís Albuquerque, Maja Bakran Marcich and more.

On today’s Brussels Playbook Podcast: Zoya and Ian discuss the summer’s hottest party: a lavish U.S. birthday celebration that’s already sparking fireworks.

**A message from YouTube: We believe in protecting kids in the digital world, not from it. That’s why we’ve spent over a decade building tailored products and protections for our youngest viewers. Our new industry-leading Shorts timer - which can be set to zero - joins bedtime and Take a Break reminders in our parental controls.**

PUSHING BACK ON THE HUAWEI PROBE: The investigation into alleged bribery that rocked the European Parliament over a year ago is fast losing steam as MEPs seek to protect their own from prosecution.

Pleading innocence: POLITICO has seen a dossier that Italian center-right MEP Fulvio Martusciello compiled to convince other lawmakers not to comply with Belgian authorities’ request to lift his immunity from prosecution, Max Griera reports.

Recap: Authorities raided more than 20 addresses and sealed two offices in the European Parliament in March 2025 as part of the probe into whether Huawei lobbyist Valerio Ottati bribed MEPs with gifts and cash — including by offering free tickets to a corporate box at Anderlecht football club that was bugged by Belgian intelligence. Huawei has always denied any wrongdoing.

Last man standing: Martusciello, the leader of Italy’s Forza Italia in the Parliament, is the last of four MEPs facing the prospect of losing his immunity. Earlier this month the legal affairs committee maintained the immunity of the other three, saying there was insufficient evidence. The dossier contains the speech Martusciello gave to the committee.  In his document sent to MEPs, Martusciello says the prosecutors’ case is built on “carelessness,” “superficiality” and easily disproven claims.

Firm denial: Martusciello denies having any relationship with Ottati, saying he had encountered him only once, and by chance. They had “never, ever” met to discuss work, he says, attaching screenshots showing six invitations Ottati sent him to Huawei events — all of which he declined.

Photographic alibi: Prosecutors cited a report by Ottati claiming he met Martusciello to discuss Huawei policy, but Martusciello says he was in Prague that day, and shows a Ryanair boarding pass and photos of him on the city’s Charles Bridge.

Bribery allegations: Martusciello denies receiving €15,000 from Huawei via a third party he called “a dear friend” to send a letter to the European Commission about 5G networks. Martusciello says he proposed the letter because the friend put forward arguments he thought were “correct.”

Transfers to his account, which prosecutors said came from Huawei’s office via this friend, were merely “refunds of cash sums” he’d sent during Covid, when his friend was stranded abroad. “Since he had a credit card and debit card limit, he sometimes ran out of money,” Martusciello says.

No favoritism: Martusciello also denies an allegation that students he recommended for the Huawei ICT Academy got preferential treatment, arguing the academy is open for everyone.

What now? Lawmakers will vote on Martusciello’s immunity Tuesday morning, amid growing irritation with Belgian authorities over a string of blunders in the Huawei probe — including wrongly attributing actions to an MEP instead of someone else with the same name, and seeking to lift Giusi Princi’s immunity before realizing she was not an MEP when the alleged conduct occurred.

WHILE YOU WERE SLEEPING: The U.S. hit Iran with a fresh wave of airstrikes, Tehran fired at American bases across the region and both sides traded claims over whether shipping can still move through the Strait of Hormuz — threatening a return to all-out war in the Middle East.

PARTY OF THE YEAR? The U.S. Embassy’s annual mega-bash has become Brussels’ hottest invitation.

TRUMP SKIPS KICKOFF: Donald Trump will not attend the U.S.’s opening World Cup game against Paraguay in Los Angeles on Friday, the tournament’s first game on U.S. soil, my colleague Sophia Cai scooped.

ISRAELI FOOD LABELS IN DOUBT: Nearly one in five food shipments labeled as Israeli and entering the EU originate from settlements in the occupied West Bank or the Golan Heights, according to a legal advocacy group.

EUCO PREVIEW: Strengthening the EU’s economy, shoring up its defense and making progress on the latest long-term budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework, are on the agenda for this month’s European Council, which kicks off on June 18. Gabriel Gavin got hold of Council President António Costa’s invitation letter.

DRONES, DRONES, DRONES: NATO allies are considering fast-tracking a drone procurement program after the Russian drone crash in Romania amplified concerns about aerial threats, Victor Jack reports.

NEW COMMISSION, NEW SKILLS? The Commission isn’t just reorganizing its departments — it’s also starting to reshape how officials are selected and promoted, with a controversial new test debuting today.

Best practices: Candidates in an internal Commission competition for posts at AD7 level will now have to pass a psychometric assessment designed to measure general cognitive abilities. A Commission spokesperson told Playbook the exercise is trialing “a new approach to internal competitions” and introduces “targeted changes, in line with established best practices in the testing industry.”

Installing a preliminary filter: According to internal communication seen by POLITICO, candidates scoring below the 60th percentile will be eliminated from the selection process.

Not just another EPSO exam: The assessment isn’t run by the European Personnel Selection Office but by SHL, a private company the Commission describes as having “recognized expertise in psychometric tests.” Candidates will have 36 minutes to answer 24 questions, measuring numerical, inductive and deductive reasoning.

Scope for expansion: For now, the test only applies to internal competitions. “But I wouldn’t be surprised if we found that it has worked really well and extended it to future competitions more broadly,” one EU official told Playbook.

Staff pushback: Unions are already sounding the alarm. “Candidates are concerned because this is a new test whose details are not entirely clear and for which the Commission claims no specific training is necessary,” said Cristiano Sebastiani, president of the Renouveau et Démocratie staff union. The union has requested detailed statistics once the first round is completed.

The Commission defended the approach, arguing to Playbook that cognitive ability “has consistently proven to be the best predictor of future job performance and measures things such as adaptability and re-trainability of candidates.”

Not everyone is convinced: Generation 2004, another staff organization, argues the test rewards speed and pattern recognition over professional expertise, institutional memory and strategic judgment. Its concern: Experienced officials who have already passed demanding EPSO competitions could see their career progression hinge on a 36-minute aptitude test.

Talks on the EU’s next long-term budget — the Multiannual Financial Framework that’ll run for seven years from 2028 — are gathering pace, with a “negotiating box” (sometimes called a “nego box”) set to be presented today. More on that lower down the email. But what actually is a nego box? It’s a list of sensitive budgetary issues that leaders have to tackle. The upcoming one will be the first time that the presidency of the Council of the EU has tinkered with figures drawn up by the Commission, so talks will be sensitive. It’s called a “box” because the talks are meant to stay on the contents of the document, rather than spin off into a wider debate.

TALK TO PLAYBOOK: Got a question for Zoya, Ian, Nick, Sarah, Dionis, Saga and the rest of the podcast team? WhatsApp us on +32 491 050629 and listen from 7 a.m. to hear if we give you a shoutout.

LOBBYING CASH: Where have all the defense lobbyists gone? According to data released today by lobby-watching NGO Corporate Europe Observatory, tech, energy and finance companies are all splashing cash on consultants and research in Brussels. Defense is at the bottom of a 15-strong list of industries that have spent more than €1 million on lobbying in the past year.

Dwarfing defense: Defense and security players declared €3.25 million in lobbying expenditure for 2025, which gets declared in 2026. That’s a fraction of the sum spent by tech (€73 million), banking and finance (€67 million) and energy (€52 million).

Playing it safe: Line Tresselt, a partner at lobby shop Rud Pedersen, reckons that’s not surprising, given the defense industry is “conservative by nature, with a long-standing focus on national markets rather than Brussels.” She told Mari Eccles: “Defense only moved decisively up the Brussels agenda after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Many defense companies are still newcomers to Brussels and have underestimated what effective EU-level engagement requires.”

Keeping it national: Tomas Dimitrov, deputy executive director at public affairs firm logos, said most defense spending is national, so “companies naturally devote a significant share of their public affairs effort to member states, where the contracts are awarded.”

Dive deeper: For more on Corporate Europe Observatory’s findings on Brussels lobbying, read our sister newsletter EU Influence, which will land in your inbox at 4 p.m.

OSLO CALLING: Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre is in Brussels on a mission to challenge the EU’s opposition to new Arctic oil and gas development. More for subscribers in Morning Energy.

BREXIT NEVER REALLY ENDS: The summit meant to herald a new chapter in U.K. and EU relations is running into trouble over a youth mobility scheme and fears of a backlash from national capitals.

RETURNS DEAL ON FAST FORWARD: The migration agreement struck last week is already moving through the European Parliament, with a committee vote expected Monday and a plenary vote potentially following on Wednesday, Hanne Cokelaere hears.

ANTI-TRUMP PRESCRIPTION: Five EU countries want governments to coordinate drug pricing policies and push back against U.S. pressure on pharmaceutical prices.

ANYONE BUT AMERICA: The EU is rushing to build closer tech alliances with countries such as Brazil and South Korea to reduce its dependence on U.S. technology.

RED FACES OVER GREEN WAIVER: Finance ministers gathering in Luxembourg today are expected to challenge the Commission’s decision to exempt green investments from the bloc’s spending rules. More for subscribers in Morning Financial Services.

CYPRUS’ MFF MOMENT: The Cyprus Council presidency is set to unveil new figures for the EU’s next seven-year budget today, Gregorio Sorgi reports.

Frugal, but not that frugal: Nicosia is expected to propose a 2 percent cut to the EU spending plan in its nego box, five EU diplomats told Morning Financial Services. That’s less than the reduction sought by Germany, the Netherlands and other northern countries.

Where the ax falls: The cuts are expected to mainly affect the European Competitiveness Fund, a €410 billion pot that finances innovative firms, and the Global Europe fund, which channels development aid, the diplomats said. The overall budget is worth nearly €2 trillion, including €166 billion in Covid-era debt repayments that won’t be amended in the nego box.

Winners: Farmers’ subsidies and regional payments — handed directly to national governments and accounting for less than half the budget — are expected to be spared, another setback for the northern camp.

Kalí týchi: Cyprus is walking a tightrope between a coalition of 16 countries pushing for more money for agriculture and regional payouts and a rival frugal camp demanding cuts of up to 15 percent. The two sides face off at a meeting of EU ambassadors on Sunday.

WEATHER: High of 17C. Sunny with a chance of rain in the afternoon.

WATCHING THE WORLD CUP: The FIFA tournament starts today with Mexico and South Africa facing off in the first match. But there’s no need to self-isolate in your living room, particularly as summer returns — fingers crossed — to Brussels. Here are some of the places that will be screening matches live:

— Place Noord, on the square in front of Brussels’ North Station, plans to screen matches during Guinguette opening hours. Entry tickets cost €5, and include a drink.

— The Belgian Red Devils’ matches will be screened in Uccle’s Wolvendael park, which also promises food trucks, bars and a DJ.

— Closer to work, Irish pub The Wild Geese is screening all big matches. Walk-ins only.

— The Ratz foodcourt in Saint Boniface promises to screen all “major” matches … while also offering free shots for every goal the Red Devils score.

— Bar du Matin in Forest is also screening matches. And while it doesn’t offer shots on the house, clients who can predict the winning team can win a €200 voucher.

And more: Other options include Au Bassin and O’Reilly’s in the city center; square Dumon at Stockel; Café Flora on the Saint-Gilles Parvis; and the Wiener square in Watermael-Boitsfort.

SPOTTED … at the lively Portugal Day celebration: the evening’s four Costas — European Council President António Costa, France’s EU Ambassador Philippe Léglise-Costa, Portugal’s EU ambassador Pedro Costa Pereira, and Brazilian Ambassador to the EU Pedro Miguel da Costa e Silva; António Costa’s Head of Cabinet Pedro Lourtie and Deputy Head of Cabinet David Oppenheimer; European Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque; former EU Ambassador to the U.K. João Vale de Almeida; the European Commission’s Telmo Baltazar and chief spokesperson Paula Pinho; Magellan Circle’s Luís Malhadinhas; Toyota’s Gonçalo Carriço; Lusa’s Brussels bureau chief Ana Matos Neves; Expresso’s Susana Frexes; the FT’s Andy Bounds and Paola Tamma; Euractiv’s Elisa Braun, Nicoletta Ionta, Victoria Becker and Eddy Wax; and POLITICO’s Zia Weise, Gregorio Sorgi, Ben Munster, Carlo Martuscelli and Gerardo Fortuna.

And the Schumaniacs, who played crowd-pleasing renditions of “Smells Like Teen Spirit” and “A Minha Casinha”: the Portuguese perm rep’s competition legal adviser Nuno Carrolo dos Santos (bass); the Dutch perm rep’s Liesbeth A Campo (vocals/keyboards); the U.K. Mission’s Maggie Ng (guitar); and former European Commission head of unit for infringement procedures René Slootjes (drums).

Also spotted … at PR firm Fourtold’s terrace summer party, eating grilled shrimp skewers and ice cream sundaes: Amazon’s Conor Sweeney; Alibaba Group’s Elias Papadopoulos; MLex’s Kait Bolongaro and Todd Buell; the Wall Street Journal’s Daniel Michaels; the European Commission’s Andreas Gahleitner; MNI’s David Thomas; Agence France-Presse’s Raziye Akkoc; ePURE’s Craig Winneker; Xylem’s Tania Pentcheva; Ecolab’s Agnese Danelon; Fourtold’s Anne-Claude Martin, Debbie Parriss, Matthew Willis, Claire Poppelwell-Scevak, Nicola Scocchi and Victoria Main; POLITICO’s Sarah Wheaton, Matthew Woelfel and Zoya Sheftalovich.

Also spotted … at a gathering of Croats working in the Brussels bubble at Grand Central: Maja Bakran Marcich, deputy director-general of DG MOVE; European Commission’s Mateo Matijević; Croatian influencer Nina Skočak; European Commission’s Head of Media in Croatia Andrea Čović Vidović; Council of the EU’s Sven Sipos; Katarina Ivanković Knežević, director for social rights and inclusion in DG EMPL; EPP adviser Leon Leskovec; Croatia’s NATO spokesperson Blanka Glasenhardt; POLITICO’s Sebastian Starcevic.

Berlin: German interior ministers face what could be their last meeting without a member of the ascendant far-right AfD at the table.

London: Keir Starmer’s government is responding to a second consecutive night of disorder on U.K. streets.

Paris: The murder of a schoolgirl has prompted an outcry over the French justice system, with Emmanuel Macron acknowledging “clear dysfunctions” and ministers promising reforms.

Washington PM: Donald Trump remains focused on Iran even as inflation speeds up.

— Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Council President António Costa receive Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.

— NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte also meets Støre. Press point at 1:15 p.m. Watch.

— Eurogroup (agenda) and European Stability Mechanism meetings in Luxembourg.

— Governing Council of the ECB meeting in Frankfurt. Press conference at 2:45 p.m. Watch.

— Democracy Commissioner Michael McGrath meets Croatia’s PM Andrej Plenković.

— Fisheries Commissioner Costas Kadis receives U.S. Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder.

— Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos meets Irish ministers Thomas Byrne and Helen McEntee.

— Executive Vice President Raffaele Fitto meets Anacláudia Rossbach, executive director of UN-Habitat.

ZDF’s Stefan Leifert; MEP Maria Walsh; former MEPs Sylvie Guillaume and José Bové; former OLAF Director-General Giovanni Kessler; Terna SpA’s Roberto Panico.
